newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU FACES CHALLENGE OVER AID, GLAVERBEL PROTESTS.
newsitem.headline: EU FACES CHALLENGE OVER AID, GLAVERBEL PROTESTS.

text.p: The European Commission, fresh from allowing another huge state bailout for France's Credit Lyonnais , is under increased pressure to clamp down on government subsidies to ailing companies in the European Union.

The campaign is being led mainly by smaller EU states -- those that even if they wanted to could not match the vast amounts of money being pumped into industries by the bloc's big countries, notably Germany and France.

Companies not being helped are also reacting in horror to the record levels of aid flowing as a result of the unification of Germany, a greater exposure to international competition and the ongoing privatisation of loss-making firms.

Luc Willame, chairman of Belgian flat glass producer Glaverbel SA , said that subsidies given to new projects in east Germany -- at a time when his sector is facing severe over-capacity -- are threatening western European companies.
"There are suspicions that the subsidies involved are beyond the level (authorised under EU state aid rules); that the investment cost is inflated," Willame told Reuters.

There are no recent figures on total subsidies granted in the 15-nation Union, but industry and Commission officials fear that statistics due soon will show that the situation has gone completely out of control.

The Commission said in its 1995 report on competition policy that the average annual aid for the Union as a whole was 94 billion European currency units ($117.5 billion), or 1.9 percent of the bloc's gross domestic product.
COMMISSION FEARS ANGRY REACTION

New figures are expected towards the end of the year, but Commission officials are keeping the prelimimary figures close to their chest, fearing angry reactions, particularly against French and German subsidies.
"Germany is the champion in all categories regarding state aid, and partticularly, aid to the manufacturing sector," one official said.

In March 1995 the Commission started an investigation into 957.1 million marks ($630 million) granted to former east German machinery giant SKET in the form of credits waiving, loan guarantees and other financial assistance.

But it was an unprecedented challenge by the German state of Saxony to the Commission's decision to block some 241 million marks promised to Volkswagen and the authorisation in September of a 3.9 billion franc ($759 million) emergency aid for Credit Lyonnais that revived the debate over state aid control.
Ireland, which took over the six-month rotating EU presidency in July has put the issue back on the agenda.
EU TREATY LEAVES ROOM FOR EXCEPTIONS
The EU treaty bans any subsidies that distort fair competition, but leaves room for many exceptions. The most common is rescue and restructuring aid if limited to bringing a firm back to profit.

A draft presidency paper calls for a reduction of the level of public subsidies and suggests that the Commission creates a register or database to keep track of all state aid decisions. The issue is expected to be discussed by EU industry ministers at their next regular meeting on November 14.
A similar proposal last year by Denmark, whose shipbuilding industry has been complaining about support given to its German rivals, found little support.

The federation of European employers, UNICE, has also called for more transparent, predictable rules, possibly modelled on the EU's successful regulation to deal with mergers and takeovers, and its strict deadlines and consultation mechanisms.

"The Commission's current procedural practice is set out...in informal communications to member states. This reinforces the perception that third parties should not be involved in the process," UNICE said in a position paper.
While European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert agrees that there is room for improvement, he warns against attempts to strip the Commission from its power to assess aid plans.

The alternative, he told a conference on competition policy, was to handle the issue to the Council of EU ministers where unanimous vote is the rule. "It would be horse trading from morning to evening", he told the Brussels think-tank the Centre for European Policy Studies.
EASTERN GERMANY SHOULD CONTINUE TO GET SUPPORT

The payment of huge subsidies in Germany is questioned by the German industry itself, although there is some consensus that the eastern regions formerly under communist rule must continue to get support.

"The exceptional situation in east Germany is fundamentally different from that of other poor regions in Europe," Ludolf von Wartenberg, secretary general of the federation of German industries (BDI) told Reuters. He argued that because the east German states were suddenly confronted with huge economic problems, rather than suffering from industrial backwardeness, they justified a special treatment for another five years.
But subsidies should go down in the western regions, von Wartenberg said, and the Commission was the only authority capable of imposing that.
"The European Commission is the only institution in Europe which has any control over the subsidy race".
